instructional_purpose: Establishes the conditional sentence as a two-slot governing frame in which a single trigger word imposes one mood on two separate verbs, and teaches the closed inventory of trigger words that do this. Pairs the syntactic rule with the class-sensitive morphology needed to actually spell the governed forms.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A trigger word of this class governs two verb positions simultaneously, not only the verb adjacent to it.
Both governed verbs surface in the jussive.

Jussive marking is realized by four different exponents depending on verb class: final sukun on sound stems, shortening of the medial long vowel on hollow stems, loss of the final weak letter on defective stems, and loss of the final nun on the suffixed dual, masculine-plural and second-feminine-singular forms.
All four trigger words belong to one category, presented under a single label translated as particles.
The human-reference trigger word simultaneously introduces the condition and supplies the subject of the condition verb.
The weak letter of a hollow or defective stem is deleted whenever the verb is jussive.
A jussive verb may surface with a short vowel rather than sukun when a following definite article would create a consonant cluster; the lesson displays this in an example without naming the repair.
One narrative example coordinates a non-jussive verb inside the condition half without comment, which the lesson does not reconcile with its own both-verbs rule.

recognition_criteria: a member of the closed trigger list stands at the opening of the clause

assign the immediately following verb to the condition slot
assign the consequence verb to the response slot
classify each verb by stem type and by whether it carries a vowel suffix
select the matching jussive exponent for each verb
for hollow and defective stems, resolve the weak letter before attaching the ending

exceptions: the lesson notes in passing that a perfect verb can carry conditional meaning, but does not treat its marking

human-reference vs. non-human-reference condition nouns
plain vs. emphatic non-human condition nouns

instructional_purpose: Decomposes the conditional sentence into its two named halves and introduces the licensing question that governs the response half: whether the response must be introduced by the connective فـ. Frames this as a decision driven by what the response opens with, and contrasts it with the bare jussive response taught in the previous lesson.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Every conditional sentence divides into a condition half and a response half, and the response half may be a clause of any type.
The response requires the connective exactly when its opening element cannot itself receive jussive marking.
There are six response-opener classes that license the connective.
After the connective followed by a future marker, the response verb carries indicative marking rather than jussive marking.
An imperative response is built on the jussive stem but constitutes a distinct mood, and therefore cannot serve as the response without the connective.
Negation words in the response impose their own mood, so the response verb cannot simply be a bare jussive.
When لم negates the condition verb, the verb is jussive by لم while the conditional trigger also governs it.
A perfect-tense response without any connective is not addressed, so the taught licensing table is not exhaustive over attested responses.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The connective is required when the response opener cannot receive jussive marking, and each of the six classes fails that test for its own reason.
A first- or third-person command response is formed with the command prefix attached to a jussive verb, and the connective precedes that whole unit.
An oath opening the response licenses the connective on the same grounds as emphatic and probability particles.
The future negator assigns the subjunctive; the past-time negator assigns the jussive but belongs to the condition half rather than the response half.

One illustrative response pairs a probability particle with a definite proper noun, a combination that is not standard for that particle.
The command prefix is described as part of the imperative construction rather than as a separate jussive-assigning particle.

instructional_purpose: Introduces direct address as a governed construction and teaches a five-way classification of the addressed noun in which the classification determines whether the noun is fixed on a damma or carries accusative marking. Adds the intermediary construction required when the addressed noun carries the definite article.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The addressed noun in direct address is classified into exactly five types, and the type determines its ending.
A single-word proper name and a specifically intended indefinite are fixed on a damma without nunation.
A non-specific indefinite, an annexation head, and a resembling-annexation head all carry accusative marking.
The definite article may not follow the address particle directly, and the intermediary construction is the required repair.
The noun following the intermediary is nominative and retains its article.
The test separating annexation from resembling-annexation is whether the second element is genitive or accusative.
A teknonym is an annexation and therefore takes accusative marking on its first element.
The construction used for an exclamatory address is presented as involving the address particle plus a prefixed lam, but the illustrating example contains no such prefix.
Address forms with the first-person possessive are glossed as noun plus possessive without stating the case they carry.
The stated ban on the definite article after the address particle is presented without its standard lexical exception.

instructional_purpose: Isolates the five suffixed imperfect conjugations whose indicative is marked by a final nun and teaches that deletion of that nun is the mood exponent for both the subjunctive and the jussive in those forms. Sets the boundary of the class by excluding the feminine plural, whose ending is superficially similar.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Exactly five imperfect conjugations end in a nun that functions as the indicative exponent.
Deletion of that nun is the exponent of both the subjunctive and the jussive for these forms.
The feminine-plural forms are not members of the set and do not vary across the three moods.
The reduced masculine-plural suffix is written with a following silent alif that is orthographic only.
The subjunctive and jussive forms of these five are identical, so the governing particle is the only cue to which mood is present.
The second-feminine-singular form belongs to the set even though it addresses one person, because membership is defined by the suffix shape.

The dual shape is listed once for the second person even though the same shape also serves the third-person feminine dual, so the count of five is a count of listed conjugations rather than of distinct surface shapes.
One row of the subjunctive-particle table gives a malformed second-feminine-singular example whose ending contradicts the rule being illustrated.
One conditional example uses dual agreement with the human-reference condition noun, which the lesson itself remarks on but does not mark as non-standard.

The explanation for why one story verb retains its nun inside a subordinate clause attributes the retention to the subordinator having no direct effect on the verb, without identifying the clause structure that actually licenses the indicative.

recognition_criteria: the imperfect verb ends in one of the three nun-bearing suffixes
in reduced form the suffix appears without its nun
a masculine-plural reduced form is followed by a silent alif
a governing subjunctive or jussive particle precedes the verb
an ending that is a nun preceded by a vowelless consonant signals the feminine plural, which is outside the set
procedures: determine the person, number and gender of the subject
decide whether the conjugation belongs to the five-member set
check for a preceding governing particle and identify the mood it assigns
delete the nun if the mood is subjunctive or jussive
add the orthographic alif after a reduced masculine-plural suffix
leave feminine-plural forms unchanged
conditions: the subject must be dual, masculine plural, or a second-person feminine singular addressee
a governing particle must be present for deletion to apply
exceptions: first-person plural and other unsuffixed forms mark mood with a final short vowel instead
contrasts: indicative with nun vs. subjunctive and jussive without it
the indicative nun vs. the feminine-plural nun, which is not a mood exponent
dual reduced forms with no alif vs. masculine-plural reduced forms with the orthographic alif
vowel-based mood marking on unsuffixed forms vs. nun deletion on suffixed forms

common_mistakes.pattern: counting the feminine-plural conjugations as members of the five-member set
common_mistakes.why_wrong: their final nun is an agreement marker, not a mood exponent, and it does not alternate across moods
common_mistakes.correction_principle: membership is defined by suffix shape; a nun preceded by a vowelless consonant is outside the set

common_mistakes.pattern: retaining the nun after a subjunctive or jussive particle
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the deletion is the mood exponent, so retaining the nun leaves the verb marked indicative under a governor that forbids it
common_mistakes.correction_principle: delete the nun whenever a subjunctive or jussive governor precedes

common_mistakes.pattern: omitting the orthographic alif after a reduced masculine-plural suffix
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the spelling convention requires it and its absence produces a form that reads as something else
common_mistakes.correction_principle: write the silent alif after the reduced masculine-plural ending

misleading_shortcuts: reading every final nun on an imperfect verb as a deletable mood exponent
expecting the reduced forms to distinguish subjunctive from jussive, when they are identical and only the governor disambiguates
treating the orthographic alif as pronounced
assuming the number of listed conjugations equals the number of distinct surface shapes

instructional_purpose: Introduces purpose clauses as a governed construction and teaches that a small set of purpose particles places the following imperfect verb in the subjunctive, including the negative purpose compounds. Adds a mood-based contrast for the particle that can express either purpose or attained result.
concepts_taught: purpose clause as a named clause type expressing the goal of an action

subjunctive government as the shared property of the set

the subjunctive exponents: final fatha on unsuffixed forms and nun deletion on suffixed forms
purpose vs. cause as a lexical contrast between two similar-looking items

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The purpose particles place the following imperfect verb in the subjunctive.
The prefixed purpose particle can be expanded with the subordinator, and the two variants are equivalent in meaning.
The purpose-or-limit particle takes the subjunctive when the goal is not yet attained and the indicative or a perfect verb when the result is attained.
Negative purpose compounds are transparent combinations of a purpose particle with the subordinator and the negator, and still govern the subjunctive.
The subjunctive exponent is a final fatha for unsuffixed forms and nun deletion for the suffixed set.
The prefixed purpose particle and the similar-looking causal particle are distinguished by function, one introducing a goal and the other a reason.

The lesson attributes the subjunctive directly to each purpose particle, without distinguishing particles that assign it themselves from particles under which a suppressed subordinator does the assigning.
Other functions of the prefixed particle and other lam constructions are not distinguished from the purpose reading.

recognition_criteria: a purpose particle stands immediately before an imperfect verb
the verb carries a final fatha where the indicative would carry a damma
a suffixed form appears without its final nun
the clause answers why the main-clause action is performed
with the purpose-or-limit particle, subjunctive marking signals the purpose reading and indicative or perfect marking signals the attained-result reading
procedures: identify the purpose particle
put the following imperfect verb in the subjunctive
select the exponent by form class: final fatha, or nun deletion for suffixed forms
for negative purpose, use one of the negative compounds and keep the subjunctive
for the purpose-or-limit particle, decide whether the goal is prospective or attained and choose the mood accordingly
conditions: the governed verb must be imperfect
the purpose reading requires the goal to be unattained at reference time
exceptions: the purpose-or-limit particle drops out of subjunctive government when it introduces an attained result
the causal particle that resembles the prefixed purpose particle does not govern the subjunctive
contrasts: purpose reading with subjunctive vs. attained-result reading with indicative or perfect
purpose particle vs. causal particle of similar shape
affirmative purpose particles vs. their negative compounds
subjunctive fatha on unsuffixed forms vs. nun deletion on suffixed forms

common_mistakes.pattern: leaving the verb after a purpose particle in the indicative
common_mistakes.why_wrong: these particles govern the subjunctive, so indicative marking leaves the verb ungoverned
common_mistakes.correction_principle: apply the subjunctive exponent after every member of the purpose set

common_mistakes.pattern: retaining the final nun on a suffixed form after a purpose particle
common_mistakes.why_wrong: for the suffixed set, nun deletion is the subjunctive exponent
common_mistakes.correction_principle: delete the nun rather than adding a vowel when the form belongs to the suffixed set

common_mistakes.pattern: treating the attained-result use of the purpose-or-limit particle as if it were purpose
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the two readings differ in whether the goal is realized, and the mood follows that difference
common_mistakes.correction_principle: decide the reading first, then select the mood

common_mistakes.pattern: substituting the causal particle for the purpose particle
common_mistakes.why_wrong: one introduces a reason for an event that occurred and the other a goal aimed at, and only the latter governs the subjunctive
common_mistakes.correction_principle: distinguish goal from cause before selecting the particle

misleading_shortcuts: treating every occurrence of the prefixed particle as a purpose marker, when the same letter serves other functions including the command prefix taught earlier in this module
treating the purpose-or-limit particle as binary, when its behaviour before an imperfect verb is a three-way distinction in fuller treatments rather than purpose versus result
assuming the subjunctive is assigned by the surface particle in every case
reading the negative compounds as unanalysable words
